articles.title: Carmarthen fossil hunter Dorothea Bate recognised with blue plaque
articles.summary: Dorothea Bate discovered the dwarf elephant and the myotragus, an extinct goat-like antelope.
articles.body:
A pioneering fossil hunter who was one of the first women to be employed by the Natural History Museum has been recognised with a national blue plaque.

Dorothea Bate, who died in 1951 aged 72, "transformed our understanding of prehistoric animals and ancient environments" through her research, Historic England said.

She has been recognised with a plaque at the Natural History Museum , in Tring, Hertfordshire, which notes in its inscription that the palaeontologist was the "Officer-in-Charge of this museum from 1948".

Bate was born in Carmarthen, Wales, in 1878 and developed a fascination with the natural world from an early age.

She moved with her family to rural Gloucestershire as a young woman and spent hours exploring the surrounding countryside and caves, collecting fossils.

She had little formal education, instead largely teaching herself, and in 1900 asked for work behind the scenes at the Natural History Museum in London.

Her determination impressed museum staff, earning her a position as an assistant and beginning an association with the institution that would last more than 50 years.

She published her first scientific paper, A Short Account Of A Bone Cave In The Carboniferous Limestone Of The Wye Valley, in 1901.

Bate went on to undertake expeditions across the Mediterranean, often travelling alone to remote caves in search of evidence of ancient life.

In Cyprus, she discovered a previously unknown species of dwarf elephant and in 1909, while in the Balearics, she discovered the myotragus - an extinct goat-like antelope.

She achieved more than 80 published scientific papers, despite spending most of her career without a permanent paid position.

In a joint statement, co-CEOs of Historic England Claudia Kenyatta and Emma Squire said that Bate's "life was defined by her intense curiosity and desire to understand the natural world".

"She used this drive to make sense of ancient life through fragments of bone, bringing it to life once again," they said.

"Her research transformed our understanding of prehistoric animals and ancient environments.

"Not only does her work continue to be invaluable in the field that she helped to establish, but as one of the first women to be employed by the Natural History Museum she was instrumental in paving the way for future women in science.

"This plaque ensures that her pioneering contributions to science receives the wider recognition it deserves."

Heritage minister Baroness Twycross said Bate's achievements "helped break through the glass ceiling and paved the way for women in palaeontology".

Dr Sandra Knapp, director of research at the Natural History Museum, said: "The role of women scientists in natural history is often hidden - but Dorothea Bate's work with fossil mammals was both innovative and set a path for others, despite obstacles.

"The installation of this plaque not only honours her but also serves as a reminder that women have been, and continue to be, key contributors to our understanding of the natural world."

articles.title: Nepal marks the 13th day of mourning after deadly flash floods
articles.summary: South Asia News: Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, 13 days after the devastating Rasuwa flash floods, as the country paid tribute to more than 1,355.
articles.body: Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, 13 days after the devastating Rasuwa flash floods, as the country paid tribute to more than 1,355 people killed in one of its deadliest natural disasters in recent history.Nearly 5,000 people remain missing, including 589 foreign nationals, following the flash floods that struck Rasuwa, a district bordering China, and neighbouring areas on August 26.The disaster was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche in the high Himalayas, unleashing powerful floodwaters that caused widespread loss of life and extensive damage to infrastructure across northern and central Nepal.According to the PTI report, Nepal has declared September 7 a national day of mourning to honour victims of the devastating floods that swept through Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other areas along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.The observance falls on the 13th day after the disaster, reflecting the traditional Hindu practice of marking the thirteenth day following a death. In many Hindu communities, the day is considered highly significant to honor the deceased members and the also mark the conclusion of the formal mourning period.The Ministry of Home Affairs said the national flag would be flown at half-mast at government offices across Nepal as well as at Nepali diplomatic missions abroad.The floods caused widespread loss of life and severe damage to homes and vital infrastructure, including roads, bridges, hydropower projects and government buildings.Search and rescue operations remain underway in the hardest-hit areas, including tunnels at hydropower projects, as security personnel and specialised international rescue teams continue efforts to locate missing people and recover bodies.At least 32,000 families have been displaced, while around 7,500 homes were completely destroyed. The disaster has also disrupted livelihoods and damaged essential infrastructure across central Nepal.The government has deployed the Nepali Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and other agencies to carry out search, rescue, relief and recovery operations.Specialist teams from neighbouring countries, including India, have joined the rescue efforts, particularly operations to save people believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels.Meanwhile, the Nepal government has declared Tuesday, September 8, a public holiday to commemorate Gen Z Martyrs’ Day, marking a year since the youth-led protests that reshaped the country’s political landscape.The protests erupted in Kathmandu on the same day last year after the government banned several social media platforms. Demonstrators also took to the streets over alleged corruption and what they described as the lavish lifestyles of the children of powerful politicians and government officials.The protests intensified after security forces opened fire near the Parliament building, killing 72 people, including children. The escalating unrest eventually prompted then-Prime Minister K P Sharma Oli to resign.The political fallout resulted in the dissolution of Parliament and the collapse of the coalition government led by the CPN-UML and Nepali Congress. A caretaker administration was subsequently installed, paving the way for fresh parliamentary elections on March 5 this year.The election brought the Gen Z-backed Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), led by Rabi Lamichhane, to power with an almost two-thirds majority. Former Kathmandu mayor Balendra Shah subsequently became prime minister.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Iran plans 'exclusion zone' near Strait of Hormuz as tensions with US flare again
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran is set to announce an “exclusion zone” around the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days and weeks, new Supreme National Security Council head Mohse.
articles.body: Iran is set to announce an “exclusion zone” around the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days and weeks, new Supreme National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei said on Sunday. The move aims at restricting vessels Tehran believes are attempting to transit the strategic waterway.Rezaei said the proposed zone would begin at the line of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, extend towards the Strait of Hormuz and continue into the Persian Gulf. Ships entering the area with the intention of passing through the strait and identified by Iran would be placed on its sanctions list.“The new zone should be announced in the coming days and weeks and “will begin from the line of the US naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf,” Rezaei said, "Any ship that enters this area with the intention of passing through the Strait of Hormuz and is identified will be placed on our sanctions list.”The announcement came a day after the United States struck three Iranian oil tankers, following Iran's launch of ballistic missiles towards US warships. Experts described the missile attacks as a dangerous escalation, particularly as Tehran's earlier attacks at sea had focused on commercial shipping.The precise location of the proposed exclusion zone remains unclear. Iran has also not specified how it would enforce the measure, which could further complicate shipping through a waterway that carries a significant share of global oil and natural gas supplies.The US military has said more than 20 warships are supporting its blockade of Iranian ports. As of Sunday, the US had redirected 92 commercial vessels and disabled three as part of efforts to prevent Iran from exporting oil.Iran on Sunday also claimed that it had struck an unmanned US vessel attempting to enter the Strait of Hormuz. The US military rejected the claim, calling it a “total lie”.Fighting resumes after weeks of relative calmThe latest escalation follows the resumption of US and Iranian attacks a week ago, after roughly a month of relative calm. The Strait of Hormuz and areas along Iran's southern coastline have again emerged as major flashpoints in the conflict, which began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes.At least five people were killed earlier this week in a US bombardment that also renewed attention on the area where a school was hit during the opening strikes of the war.The Trump administration has increasingly pursued a two-pronged strategy, combining military action against Iranian attacks around the strait with pressure on foreign financial institutions accused of handling Iranian funds.Iran's new hard-line leadership, meanwhile, has indicated that Tehran is prepared to withstand further pressure. The country has spent decades developing ways to evade sanctions and has continued finding routes to sell its oil despite the US blockade of its ports.Iran seeks guarantees before renewed diplomacyRezaei also expressed scepticism about efforts to revive negotiations with Washington, including the role of countries that have acted as mediators.The memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in mid-June began to unravel within days, with both sides accusing the other of violating its terms.“We had trusted our friends in Pakistan, Qatar or Oman, thinking that since they had stepped in as mediators, one of a mediator’s responsibilities is that if one side violates the agreement, they should stop them,” Rezaei said. “We are now pursuing diplomacy with guarantees.”The comments suggest that Tehran is seeking stronger assurances before considering another diplomatic process with Washington, as fighting and economic pressure continue.Strait remains crucial to global energy suppliesThe Strait of Hormuz remains one of the world's most important energy corridors, with the conflict disrupting the movement of oil and gas tankers through the waterway.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that around 9 million barrels of oil a day were still passing through the strait, a figure he said could help ease pressure on global energy prices. Wright told CNN that, with oil also moving through regional pipelines, flows were “probably two-thirds or more of preconflict flows.”Those shipments, however, depend heavily on the presence of US naval forces escorting tankers and providing protection against possible Iranian attacks. Wright said he expected other countries to eventually support the US Navy's efforts.Rezaei, meanwhile, sought to portray Iran's oil trade as largely unaffected by the blockade.“Every day we are selling one million, one and a half million (barrels), as if Iran’s oil production and trade are continuing as usual.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pre-loved uniforms save Coventry families £69, says charity
articles.summary: Clothing Coventry has helped provide thousands of children with second-hand school uniform.
articles.body:
Thousands of families saved money on school uniforms this summer through a charity scheme providing pre-loved and donated clothing for free.

Katie Wilson, CEO of Clothing Coventry, said parents were able to select items they needed and families saved an average of £69 by going to its uniform events that ran across three weeks.

Wilson said the average cost of a school uniform is estimated at £249.58 per child and that "remains a real challenge" for many families, and the charity has helped more than 2,700 children prepare for the new school year.

"Projects like this only happen because people give their time, resources and support - thank you to every volunteer who joined us," she added.

Across the events, the charity distributed 15,005 uniform items, including:

Alongside donated and pre-loved uniforms, it also supplied 4,659 brand-new items to 2,142 children.

A further 60 families received £30 uniform vouchers when the charity was unable to provide a blazer for their child's school.

Wilson said blazers and logoed PE kits were among the most requested items, and despite additional purchases and generous donations, demand outstripped supply in some cases.

"We could have given out probably 600 blazers if we had them, we didn't have enough to help everyone who came.

"The hope is that we can help everyone with a little bit of something" she told BBC CWR.

The programme, now in its fourth year, is supported by Coventry Building Society.

"While we can never guarantee every item, in every size, for every school, we are proud to say that no family who attended our events left empty-handed," Wilson said.

One parent who used the service said getting uniforms for their children had been a major concern.

"As a family with eight children and a very limited income, getting school uniforms for all our children was a big worry for us," they said.

"The support we received made a huge difference and took away a lot of financial stress.

"It helped us make sure our children could go back to school with the uniforms they needed. We are truly grateful to everyone who made this possible."

Clothing Coventry will reopen for school uniform requests on 14 September and said families can access uniform support throughout the year, not just during the summer holidays.

articles.title: Brazil's Porto Seguro is paying $10 for each captured lionfish; nearly 500 have been removed as they threaten native reefs and local fisheries
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The municipality of Porto Seguro, Brazil, is paying $10 for each captured lionfish, which has invaded the region's waters and threatened native specie.
articles.body: The municipality of Porto Seguro, Brazil, is paying $10 for each captured lionfish, which has invaded the region's waters and threatened native species. Nearly 500 of the invasive fish have been removed from the sea far south of Bahia, in about a month after the invasion, and brought to the Fishermen's Colony in areas outside of the Recife de Fora Marine Natural Park. Authorities are attempting to control a venomous predator that reproduces rapidly, threatening local reefs, native fish, crustaceans and fisheries, according to a report by CPG.Lionfish are native to the Indo-Pacific and have found favourable conditions to spread throughout the Atlantic Ocean. Combined with their high reproductive capacity and few natural control mechanisms, they have further invaded areas that support their expansion. Moreover, they do not have a specific diet. They can consume various marine organisms, including small fish, crustaceans and other prey. They are also not restricted to a specific habitat and can occupy reefs, rocky areas, mangroves and other marine environments.Not just aquatic members, they also pose a risk to people who come into contact with the fish. An adult lionfish can have up to 18 venomous spines distributed across its fins that function as a defence mechanism. If someone touches, steps on or attempts to handle them, their sting can lead to intense pain and nausea.In 2022, the Department of Health of Ceará recorded a case involving a 24-year-old fisherman. The fisherman stepped on a lionfish and suffered seven stings to the foot, leading to intense pain, fever and convulsions.Alert for invasionThe alert in Porto Seguro intensified on June 12, 2026, when the first official occurrence of the lionfish was recorded in the Recife de Fora Marine Natural Park. Shortly after, new specimens began to appear, prompting local authorities to expand their response. Now, lionfish are being captured for $10 each in an operation involving local fishermen and the Municipal Department of Environment and Animal Causes, known as Semac. The measure is temporary and is part of actions directed at areas outside the Recife de Fora Marine Natural Park.The strategy is aimed at curbing the numbers before the species is widely established in the area. According to sources, the sooner an invasive species is identified and controlled, the greater are the chances of reducing its impacts. Porto Seguro has developed a Municipal Action Plan to tackle lionfish. The document encompasses measures for monitoring, capture, scientific research, training, and accident prevention.The specimens are not just being removed but also being used as scientific material. The priority is to send them to the Marine Ecology and Conservation Laboratory of the Federal University of Southern Bahia, Lecomar/UFSB. In the laboratory, the animals can be weighed, measured, and analysed.The analyses seek to understand how the invasion is establishing itself along the Bahia coastline. Researchers are investigating diet, genetics, origin, behaviour, and distribution of the captured fish. This information helps identify where the species is concentrating and which native organisms appear in its diet.Spreading across the regionSurprisingly, the presence of this species is not restricted to Porto Seguro. In August 2026, the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation or ICMBio, confirmed lionfish in the Abrolhos Marine National Park, also along the Bahia coastline. The area is home to significant biodiversity and South Atlantic coral reef formations.Following the record in Abrolhos, ICMBio reported that it began taking action in partnership with other institutions. The actions include monitoring and management of the species, given the concern over the lionfish’s ability to continue advancing along the Brazilian coast.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years
articles.summary: The cuts come as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.
articles.body:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.

The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.

JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.

Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process.

"The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.

JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.

The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save £1.7bn over the next two years.

JLR is "as strategically important as it gets for the UK economy", according to David Bailey, business and economics professor at Birmingham University.

He said many UK jobs were dependent on its supply chain and the economy as a whole took a hit when the firm closed down production because of last year's cyberattack.

"It's the centre of our automotive industry," he added.

Yet, the car maker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.

In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.

In its results for the year to the end of March, JLR said US tariffs and the cyberattack were the main reasons why its sales had slumped by a fifth to £22.9bn from £29bn in the previous two years.

Ian Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US.

"The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.

He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party in terms of producing their first electric car which is just about to go into production".

Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".

The prime minister's official spokesman said: "We understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and the wider communities."

The spokesman added that Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds "is in close contact with JLR and he will be meeting them early this week", but ruled out "any form of bailout".

Business and trade committee chair Liam Byrne called the cuts a "body blow for workers, families and communities across the West Midlands".

"Whether or not these redundancies are voluntary, we now need urgent assurances that maximum support will be deployed to help everyone affected find new work," he added.

Some have blamed the issues facing JLR and the wider UK car industry on the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which was introduced by the previous Conservative government and kept under Labour.

It requires that all new car and van sales in the UK must be zero emission vehicles by 2035, but it does not apply to cars sold overseas, which is where JLR makes most of its revenue.

Shadow transport secretary Richard Holden said the ZEV mandate and higher energy costs were "crippling the British automotive industry", pledging to scrap the mandate.

At the weekend, the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham, said the ZEV mandate was "unsustainable" and that the UK car industry had suffered from "years of underinvestment" under both Labour and the Conservatives.

"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said over the weekend.

The UK Sustainable Investment and Finance Association has defended the ZEV mandate, previously calling it "crucial for attracting finance into this infrastructure as it sets out a clear, predictable pathway for the growth of the electric vehicle market".

articles.title: In 1894, a 4,000-sq-ft Illinois Victorian was built; 132 years later, a 67-year-old retiree bought it for $97,500 and has already spent $85,000 restoring just 1,000 sq ft
articles.summary: US News: Rebecca Roucloux Avery, 67, had already done the thing most people aspire to: she owned a brand-new home in Austin, a city people pay premiums to move.
articles.body: Rebecca Roucloux Avery, 67, had already done the thing most people aspire to: she owned a brand-new home in Austin, a city people pay premiums to move to. She was retired, financially stable, and living in a modern construction built to last. But then she left it all for a 132-year-old Victorian home in Vermont, a small town in Illinois, according to a report by Realtor.com. Worse, she spent nearly as much money fixing the place as she'd paid for it in the first place.For Avery, leaving Austin wasn't about the house. It was about the people in it. She wanted to be closer to her family. So the proximity to progress really mattered less. And that’s exactly when she stumbled onto something that felt like destiny wrapped in red brick and a mansard roof. Along with her partner, she is renovating the Victorian home built in 1894. They have already fixed up 1,000 square feet. Four months into ownership, with the foundation and the roof fixed, she is learning how expensive it can be to restore old homes. There’s more to do, but Avery is someone who loves a project, so it's keeping her busy.A Facebook post changed everythingAvery didn't want to spend her whole life in Texas. That's when she saw an old Victorian house made of brick with a mansard roof. "It looked like the Herman Munster house. It wasn’t even for sale," she told the outlet. She always wanted to live in a big, old Victorian house, as she loves history and architecture. As Vermont has its own Facebook page, Avery posted about the Victorian house she was interested in. "I asked if anyone knew of any houses for sale. People responded, letting me know about a house that was two blocks away from the one I was first interested in," she recalled.It was a 4,000-sq-ft home, and the asking price was $125,000. Her son paid a visit and found it had a new roof and a nice basement. The sellers were ready for a handshake deal at $110,000. She thought it was a great bargain, given that it could be sold for $200,000.She continued looking for other homes, and that's when she stumbled upon the one she bought. The 4,000-sq-ft home sits on half an acre. The Victorian house has five bedrooms and two-and-a-half bathrooms. She called the owner directly, and he revealed that he bought the house seven years ago at an auction for $10,000. The house was already deteriorating. The roof had leaked for years. There was no air conditioning, no kitchen. A basement fire had left its own damage. The asking price was $160,000. Her realtor, Nick Curtis, helped coordinate a proper inspection of the Victorian house, and she negotiated the seller down from $160,000 to $97,500. He had an insurance claim on the roof he'd never pursued; she leveraged that. He agreed to $10,000 worth of foundation work during the inspection period. But the renovation work was only about to begin. Foundation work ran $45,000. The roof and rotted decking cost another $40,000. These were the big-ticket items, the ones she'd been warned about. But they weren't the only surprises.“When we repaired the roof, we closed off the chimney. That accidentally trapped some bats inside that came flying out while I was on the couch watching TV. The second issue was water. The basement flooded after a big rain. We needed a sump pump. It took 12 hours to get the water out – I was crying. The last thing was a weird design quirk. The third floor had a balcony that opened up and overlooked a bathroom and a giant garden tub. We sheetrocked over that and made the balcony space a closet,” Avery told the outlet.Despite all the trouble, Avery is happy, as she feels this is the house meant for her. "It was the right house for us. This home makes sense because my partner and I can do the renovation work. He has done some electrical work already, helping remove the knob-and-tube wiring. I am handling the design and have put in a lot of hours removing wallpaper, skim-coating walls, and sanding. I have spent 40 hours on one bedroom alone," she said.They're not trying to flip this house. They're not even sure it's their forever home: at 4,000 square feet, it's twice the size of what she needs, and the stairs feel steeper every year. But this home is everything she has hoped for. Neighbours walk by regularly now, stopping to ask about the renovation. She's invited about 20 people inside to see the transformation. They tell her how gorgeous it's becoming, how grateful they are that someone is saving this piece of their town's history. She has found a community, and she is happy. After all, home is where the heart is. In the end, that's what matters the most, right?Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nepal holds national day of mourning for victims of flash flood disaster
articles.summary: Flags flew at half mast on the 13th day since the disaster, the last day of the Hindu mourning period.
articles.body:
Nepalis observed a national day of mourning for the victims of the flash flood on Monday, lighting candles to mark the last day of the traditional 13-day Hindu mourning period.

While flags were flown at half mast, commemorations were scaled back as rescue teams continue to search for survivors. Candlelight vigils were planned for Monday evening.

At least 1,287 people are known to have died after a flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through villages in a Himalayan valley along border between Nepal and Tibet.

Almost two weeks later, more than 5,000 people are still missing.

Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency that there would be "no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas."

Nepal's president, Ram Chandra Paudel, toured areas devastated by the floods on Monday, an aide told Reuters.

The home ministry said that government offices, as well as missions abroad, would fly the national flag at half mast to mark the final day of the mourning period.

Army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Agence France-Presse that rescue efforts were continuing "with the same tempo we had on day one".

"Our focus is on search and rescue at three levels - on ground, by air, and in the tunnels," he said.

"We are making sure that no one is still stranded."

Among the few places where rescuers still see a chance of finding survivors is in tunnels that form part of the region's hydropower stations, with hundreds of workers among the missing.

Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said in an update on X that the operation meant facing "multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved."

Four people have been rescued in recent days, three at hydropower stations or tunnels.

On Saturday, a 64-year-old Nepali woman was pulled from her buried house on Saturday, more than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud partially buried her house in the Nuwakot district.

She was discovered alive on the fourth floor of the building by Nepal's Armed Police Force and airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment.

On Sunday rescue workers in China recovered twelve bodies in the Nepal-Tibet border, using excavators, shovels and ground penetrating radar at the site.

At least 5,083 people are still missing in Nepal. On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.

articles.title: Trump admin again urges Supreme Court to restrict mail-in voting as midterms approach
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration is urging the Supreme Court to enforce new mail-in voting restrictions just before the critical November midterm elections, citing concerns over ballot distribution and potential confusion.
articles.body: The Trump administration has asked the US Supreme Court to allow new mail-in voting restrictions to take effect before states send millions of ballots for November’s congressional elections.The emergency request, filed Sunday, asks the Supreme Court to lift a federal court order blocking a US Postal Service rule that would impose new requirements on mail ballots.US District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston extended the block on Friday, prompting the administration to return to the Supreme Court with a fresh application.Solicitor General John Sauer argued that keeping the restrictions on hold could create uncertainty as states begin distributing ballots. He warned that every day the injunction remains in place “risks sowing confusion and chaos” as more voters receive mail ballots.Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has given opponents until Wednesday to respond to the administration’s request.The dispute comes as the November 3 midterm elections approach. North Carolina became the first state to mail ballots for the election on Friday, meaning the timing of the Supreme Court’s decision could affect states already moving ahead with postal voting.The Postal Service rule was introduced to implement an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in March. It would require states to provide USPS with lists of voters receiving mail ballots, while ballot envelopes would have to carry unique barcodes.USPS would also be permitted to reject ballots that do not meet the new requirements or that are linked to voters missing from the lists.The administration had previously asked the Supreme Court to intervene after Talwani issued an earlier, temporary injunction. Before the justices ruled on that request, the judge extended the restriction on Friday, prompting Sunday’s new filing.Mail-in voting is available in every US state, although the rules vary. Twenty-nine states allow voters to request a mail ballot without giving a reason, while eight states conduct elections entirely by mail.Trump has repeatedly called for tighter controls on mail voting and has made unsubstantiated claims that widespread fraud was responsible for his defeat in the 2020 presidential election.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: New Inbetweeners film confirmed by Netflix as lead stars return
articles.summary: Netflix has confirmed the original stars of the coming-of-age sitcom are set to reprise their roles for the film.
articles.body:
Ooh, sequel friend! A new Inbetweeners movie is officially in the works, Netflix has confirmed.

The original cast of Simon Bird, James Buckley, Blake Harrison and Joe Thomas will reprise their roles for the feature film, with production starting on Monday.

The Inbetweeners 3 will follow on the story of their characters, Will McKenzie, Jay Cartwright, Neil Sutherland and Simon Cooper.

They originally starred in three seasons of the popular coming-of-age sitcom, which aired on E4 between 2008 and 2010.

It followed their trials and misadventures as suburban teenagers at the fictional Rudge Park Comprehensive as they navigated school life and friendship.

The show has gained new fans over the years due to some of its best bits finding new life on social media, as well as through the film sequels.

The third instalment follows two sequels backed by Film4, which were released in 2011 and 2014.

Alongside the announcement, Netflix released a teaser video which showed Will, Simon, Neil and Jay return to their iconic yellow Fiat.

The friend group all get into the tiny car but Simon struggles to start the engine.

After some encouragement, it gets going and they drive out of what looks like a storage unit.

Production kicks off after months of speculation that there would be another film, but beyond the lead characters returning, the rest of the cast is yet to be confirmed.

Fans will be wondering if English actress Emily Atack will return in her role as Charlotte Hinchcliffe, or if Emily Head will come back as Carli D'Amato.

However, Netflix has announced The Inbetweeners creators, Damon Beesley and Iain Morris, will return to write and direct the film.

Beesley and Morris said it has been "super fun" hanging out with friends again.

"We're going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans," they added.

The first film sees the group of friends head to Crete in Greece for a post sixth form break, but they quickly find more trouble than they bargained for.

The 2014 follow-up reunites Will, Simon, and Neil as they travel to Australia to visit Jay during his gap year - where they find out his travels aren't as lavish as his messages had claimed.

Tensions rise as they clash over whether to chase cultural experiences or a wilder time on their trip.

The first film made history as the biggest opening weekend for a UK comedy at the time, according to Netflix, while the sequel also broke box office records.

articles.title: Coop win appeal against paying £600k to former boss
articles.summary: Appeal judges ruled it was not reasonably foreseeable Colin MacLeod may be psychiatrically injured.
articles.body:
The Channel Islands Coop has won an appeal against paying its former chief executive £600,000 in a compensation payout.

Colin MacLeod won a court case against the Coop last year , claiming the company had treated him unfairly, leaving him with a psychiatric injury. The Coop challenged the decision.

In May, judges originally ruled Coop would have to pay the £600,000 despite the appeal against the ruling not being heard.

On 1 September, three appeal judges sided with the Coop, accepting MacLeod was subjected to an unfair and inappropriate campaign by some directors, but that it was "not reasonably foreseeable that he would sustain a psychiatric injury" as a result of the situation.

MacLeod, who was chief executive of the Coop for 10 years, described the legal battle with the company as "long and excruciating" last December.

The court upheld that there had been a "deliberate campaign" to remove MacLeod and that the conduct of three directors "constituted bad faith".

This included meeting in secret without maintaining records, failing to raise concerns through formal channels and two expenses audits being targeted at MacLeod.

The Coop won the appeal against paying MacLeod £600,000 because he was a "strong personality" with "no known pre-existing vulnerability or susceptibility to psychiatric harm".

The court said, while it would have been foreseeable, MacLeod would have been "distressed, upset and angry" it was not "reasonably foreseeable that he would sustain a psychiatric injury".

The court therefore overturned the Royal Court's finding of liability.

articles.title: Cardiff man hit with 'death tax' after inheriting mother's home
articles.summary: Phil Bond says he fears people in the same situation may pay the charge without challenging it.
articles.body:
A bereaved man says he has been hit with a "death tax" after inheriting his mother's home.

Phil Bond, 68, lost his mother, Eunice, 91, in May and inherited her house in Cardiff, alongside his brother.

Soon after her death, they received a council tax bill that included a charge for "premium furnished and no-one resident", doubling the annual amount owed to more than £4,000.

In Wales, local authorities can charge a council tax premium of up to 300% on furnished second homes that his mother's property had been reassigned as.

Cardiff Council said no council tax exemption was applied automatically following a resident's death, but circumstances could be considered on request.

In Cardiff a 100% premium applies to furnished properties that are not anyone's sole or main residence.

The premium is intended to encourage bringing empty homes back into use, helping to increase the availability of housing and support sustainable communities.

But Bond, from Llandaff North, said this premium felt like both a "penalty" and a "death tax".

He added: "What I find amazing is the way it's set up, as if the council expects you to empty the house straightaway and then worry about the funeral after."

Bond said that after his mother's death he was occupied with informing friends and family and organising the funeral - the house was "the last thing on my mind".

He added: "Once the funeral is over and everything starts to come back to reasonably normal we then start to look to clear the house because we're going to sell it so we go through everything and then this bombshell drops."

Bond said that he did not object to paying council tax at his mother's property, but it was purely the extra charge he objected to.

He was able to get an exemption after contacting local councillors but is still on the hook for a reduced premium of £544 for the period between May and August when the house was furnished.

He said the premium still felt like a "death tax" and the family were being "penalised through no fault of ours".

Bond added: "You can't tell me we're the first people that this has affected. Someone somewhere has ended up in the same situation."

Cardiff Council said it was sorry to hear of the family's loss and it aimed to make residents aware of any council tax reductions or exemptions.

"There is no council tax exemption that is applied automatically following the death of a resident," a spokesperson told the Local Democracy Reporting Service.

"Where a person who lived alone has died the property may be exempt from council tax if it remains unoccupied.

"This exemption remains in place until probate or letters of administration have been granted unless that process takes longer than two years.

"Once probate or letters of administration have been granted the exemption can continue for a further 12 months.

"Where probate or letters of administration are not required, council tax remains payable by the owner or occupier in the usual way."

The council said "substantially unfurnished" properties may be exempt from council tax for up to six months.

Properties that are "actively being marketed for sale" are exempt from the premium and are charged only the standard rate of council tax for up to 12 months.

Residents who believe they may qualify for a reduction or exemption are encouraged to contact the council "so that their circumstances can be considered".

articles.title: 'Kept on ventilator': Congress flags delay in proroguing Parliament, links it to delimitation Bills
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Congress on Monday questioned the delay in proroguing Parliament’s Monsoon Session, with party general secretary Jairam Ramesh alleging tha.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Monday questioned the delay in proroguing Parliament’s Monsoon Session, with party general secretary Jairam Ramesh alleging that the government was keeping the session open while seeking the numbers needed to pass the Delimitation Bills.Parliament’s Monsoon Session began on July 20 and was adjourned sine die on August 13 after 19 sittings. Ramesh said 25 days had passed since the adjournment, but Parliament had still not been prorogued.“Today is exactly 25 days since Parliament was adjourned sine die. But it has still NOT been prorogued,” Ramesh said in a post on X.He said prorogation normally takes place three to four days after a session is adjourned sine die, while citing the 28-day gap during the 2015 Monsoon Session as an earlier example.Ramesh links delay to delimitation BillsRamesh referred to the 2015 session, which he said had been largely disrupted over the Lalit Modi issue. He alleged that the then Modi government had kept that session alive in the hope of passing the GST Bills, which required a two-thirds majority in the Rajya Sabha.He said the government was subsequently forced to consult the opposition more meaningfully before the Bills were passed later.Ramesh alleged that this year’s Monsoon Session was being kept open because the Union home minister was seeking a two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha for the Delimitation Bills.“The 2026 Monsoon Session has been kept on ventilator because the home minister is still scrambling around for his super-tainted two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha to get the Delimitation Bills passed,” he said.“How much longer before he accepts the reality that his politics of threats and intimidation has reached its limit?” Ramesh added.The remarks came after the government faced a setback in the Lok Sabha in April over a Constitution Amendment Bill related to delimitation and implementation of women's reservation.What happened during the Monsoon SessionDuring the Monsoon Session, 12 bills were passed by Parliament, while 11 bills were introduced in the Lok Sabha and two in the Rajya Sabha.Only the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, was debated in the House, while the remaining Bills were passed without discussion amid opposition protests over issues including the NEET paper leak, alleged theft of Ram Temple donations and the police action against student protesters on July 20.The opposition had repeatedly disrupted proceedings during the session.Earlier setback for delimitation BillThe government had faced a setback on April 17 when a Constitution Amendment Bill involving delimitation for implementation of women's reservation in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies was defeated in the Lower House.528 MPs voted on the Bill, with 298 supporting it and 230 opposing it. A two-thirds majority required 352 votes.The defeat had raised questions over the government's ability to secure the numbers required for constitutional amendments related to delimitation.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Kenya minister warns foreigners against 'misusing' visas to trade
articles.summary: Kenya is due to start enforcing measures to restrict foreign nationals from operating small-scale businesses.
articles.body:
Kenya's trade ministry has warned foreign nationals that visa-free entry into the country does not grant them the right to work, as the government vows to shut down unlicensed small businesses run by foreigners.

President William Ruto had set today as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work.

Ahead of the move, the Burundian embassy in Kenya said it would offer emergency free travel documents to its citizens willing to go back home, amid reports of the mistreatment of Burundians.

It is unclear how many foreign nationals are involved in small-scale trading or how many would be affected by the crackdown.

In a statement, the trade ministry said there was a "deliberate misuse of visa applications by some visitors", adding that some entered Kenya as investors or tourists but then got involved in business activities in breach of their declared status.

"Owing to the high number of foreigners involved in the retail and local trade sectors, there is therefore a need to align their activities and ensure compliance with work permit provisions," Trade Minister Lee Kinyanjui said.

Last week, Ruto said that Kenya remained open to foreign investment, but it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop".

He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.

Ruto's comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation.

Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change".

"Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added.

Bizimana's post followed an urgent meeting he held with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region.

Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group. Kenyan representatives attended the meeting called by Bizimana in Burundi.

Bizimana said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse.

On Sunday, a top official in Kenya's foreign affairs ministry said foreigners, with the required documentation, including "work permits and licences", could continue their activities.

"Burundian nationals and all East Africans - and Africans for that matter - are free to live in Kenya as long as they conduct their businesses or work according to the requirements of our laws, Permanent Secretary Korir Sing'oei said.

The government's clarification, however, did little to ease concerns among some foreign traders.

Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient.

He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans are also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries.

"This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda."

Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police.

articles.title: Man who murdered Orkney waiter to have conviction reviewed
articles.summary: Michael Ross was found guilty of shooting Shamsuddin Mahmood in an Orkney restaurant in 1994.
articles.body:
A former soldier serving a life sentence for the murder of a waiter in Orkney in 1994 is to have his conviction re-examined.

Shamsuddin Mahmood, 26, was shot in the head at point-blank range as he served customers in an Indian restaurant in Kirkwall.

Michael Ross - who was just 15 at the time - was convicted in 2008 after he joined the Army and became a sniper. He has always maintained his innocence.

A previous bid by Ross to have the case reviewed by the Scottish Criminal Cases Review Commission (SCCRC) was rejected in 2014 .

The case will be looked at again and could ultimately be referred back to the courts.

The SCCRC said it was restricted by law in terms of the information it could disclose about the cases it reviews.

However, it confirmed to BBC Scotland News that the commission had received an application from Ross which had now been accepted for a review.

Mahmood was shot and killed in front of diners, including young children, after a masked man walked into the Mumutaz restaurant.

The death of the Bangladeshi national and university graduate shocked the island community and beyond.

The prime suspect at the time was 15-year-old schoolboy Ross, but without sufficient evidence the case went cold.

Ross went on to become a sniper in the Black Watch and was decorated for his actions in Iraq.

Then, 12 years after Mahmood was murdered, a new witness came forward.

It resulted in Ross being charged and tried at the High Court in Glasgow in June 2008.

He was found guilty and sentenced to life in prison, with a minimum sentence of 25 years.

But his conviction was overshadowed by an audacious escape attempt.

As he was about to be led away Ross knocked over a security guard, and jumped out of the dock.

He pulled open a side door but was eventually stopped in a court corridor.

The following day, a hire car was discovered parked in a supermarket car park in Springburn.

Inside was a cache of weapons including a loaded machine gun, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, a grenade, and a hunting knife.

articles.title: Four murder arrests over baby's death in Staffordshire woodland
articles.summary: Police say they have arrested two men and two women as part of their investigation.
articles.body:
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a baby was found dead while camping with her family in Staffordshire.

The three-month-old girl died after emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest in woodland off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, at 08:45 BST on Saturday.

The people arrested were a 42-year-old man and 30-year-old woman from south Staffordshire, a 20-year-old woman from Wolverhampton and an 18-year-old man from Walsall.

All four were detained at the scene and have since been bailed while inquiries continue, Staffordshire Police said.

Det Insp Josh Lee said officers were working to gather further evidence around the circumstances of the girl's death and were "keeping an open mind".

He said it was being treated as an isolated incident and urged people not to share "unconfirmed and speculative" claims online.

The scene of the tragedy was described as being "hidden away" from the main woodland in the Wyrley and Essington Branch Canal Local Nature Reserve.

It is not an official camping site but locals said people would often fish in two nearby pools, while the nature trail is also popular with dog walkers and runners.

Officers were in the area over the weekend to provide reassurance to the community and a bunch of roses was left nearby in tribute to the girl.

A cordon was in place around the scene, close to the fishing lake, where two camping tents had been pitched.

Residents living in Cheslyn Hay, which has a population of about 7,000 people, were said to have been left shocked by the child's death.

Councillor Robert Duncan, of South Staffordshire Council, said the community was devastated and urged residents to "avoid speculation".

People should "allow the family and responders the privacy and respect they deserve", he added.

The superintendent of the Cannock Chase Methodist Church Circuit, Rev Samantha Hagerman, said: "Our thoughts and prayers are with family, friends and emergency services affected by the incident near Cheslyn Hay yesterday."

Sir Gavin Williamson, MP for Stone, Great Wyrley and Penkridge, described it as "extremely distressing news" which had caused a lot of concern in the area.

He also called for people not to speculate about what happened and to allow police to carry out their investigations.

"I am extremely grateful to the emergency services and my thoughts are with the child's family at this incredibly upsetting time," he said on Facebook.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's sister pleads for end to 'AI garbage' posts after singer's death
articles.summary: Since Parton's death in late August, dozens of AI-generated songs, images and videos have appeared online.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton's sister has issued a plea to fans over "fake AI garbage" posted on social media in the wake of the singer's death.

Tributes to the late country legend have appeared online and at locations including the Country Music Hall of Fame in Nashville, after Parton died on 25 August at the age of 80.

Writing on Instagram, Stella Parton thanked those who had shown "genuine support" for the star and her family - but said a "tremendous amount of AI and endless garbage being posted" had been "challenging to absorb".

Her request for people to show "more compassion" in how they respond to Parton's death follows similar pleas from families of late celebrities over AI tributes.

In October, Robin Williams' daughter asked fans to stop sending fake AI-generated videos of her father .

Zelda Williams' plea was shared by Dr Martin Luther King Jr's daughter Bernice A King, who asked fans to "please stop" in a post on Instagram.

Little over a month later, Robert Redford's daughter Amy spoke out over AI content created to pay tribute to the American actor following his death last September.

"Every human being experiences pain and loss in life and my family is no different," wrote Parton in her Instagram post on Friday .

"Sadly, because of the way our lives have been lived in front of the public, we have no choice but to be subjected to incredible pressure and insensitivity from strangers."

She said there had been a tide of AI and "garbage" posts, adding: "As time passes, those who are in the business of exploiting the loss and tragedies of others on a daily basis will move onto the next stampede of endless misinformation."

Parton also asked that people look to her sister's life as "an example for tolerance" and mutual respect.

"It's not about the most clever comments, fake AI garbage or snarky tweets," she said.

With an abundance of AI tools able to quickly generate text, images, video or audio, many have used them to craft tribute posts for departed stars.

Since Parton's death in late August, dozens of AI-generated songs, images and videos have appeared online.

US President Donald Trump was among those to share such material - posting an AI-generated image of himself and Parton, arm in arm, on his platform Truth Social .

Another image criticised as an AI fake, shared on Instagram and X, depicted the late country singer without any make-up or a wig.

One X user described it as "incredibly weird", while another called it a "violation".

On YouTube, a "heartfelt fan-made tribute by Miley Cyrus" to her godmother Dolly Parton and sung in the style of the Wrecking Ball singer has had more than 1.5 million views.

It has an AI label and disclaimer in the description to say it is not an "official release by Miley Cyrus or Dolly Parton's representatives".

But scores of comments have been left on the video thanking Cyrus for the "perfect tribute".

Other AI-generated tributes in the style of singers Pink and Celine Dion have also been widely-viewed online.

And Dolly Parton herself appeared to have been concerned about the potential impact of AI on artists.

She told The Hollywood Reporter in 2023 that while she thought AI was "going to be great for a lot of things, like science and medicine", the idea of it replacing humans "scares me".

"That's like the mark of the beast. It's like you can't remake a person," she said.

"I want to just leave a body of work behind. I think all this stuff can be great, used in the right way.

"But not to replace voices and writings and not to replace a human being that belongs to God."

articles.title: “Perfect for this kind of human being”: Celeste Rivas Hernandez's family calls for D4vd death penalty
articles.summary: US Streamers News: The family of Celeste Rivas Hernandez has spoken about the punishment they want D4vd to face if he is convicted of murdering the teenager. As Septembe.
articles.body: The family of Celeste Rivas Hernandez has spoken about the punishment they want D4vd to face if he is convicted of murdering the teenager. As September 7, 2026, marks what would have been Celeste's 16th birthday, her family said it supports the death penalty in the case. They made strong comments about the singer while speaking to the New York Post. However, the final decision on whether to seek the death penalty will be made by prosecutors and the California justice system.Celeste Rivas Hernandez's family supports death penalty for D4vdCeleste's family said it believes the death penalty would be the right punishment for D4vd if he is convicted. Speaking to the New York Post, the family said, “If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being.”The family also described the person responsible for Celeste's death as someone who was “devoid of feelings” and “without conscience.”However, they also said that the final decision is not theirs to make. The family said the matter is now in the hands of God and the California justice system.Their comments came just before what would have been Celeste's 16th birthday. Celeste was 14 years old when prosecutors say she was killed in April 2025.Prosecutors have yet to decide whether D4vd will face death penaltyD4vd, whose real name is David Anthony Burke, has been charged with first-degree murder with special circumstances. Because of the charges against him, prosecutors can consider seeking the death penalty.Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman said last week that the death penalty is still an option in the case. However, his office has not yet made a final decision.Prosecutors allege that D4vd killed Celeste in April 2025 after she allegedly threatened to expose their illegal sexual relationship. They also allege that he later dismembered her body and placed her remains in bags.Celeste's remains were later discovered inside a Tesla at a Hollywood impound lot in September 2025, according to prosecutors.A judge ordered D4vd to stand trial in July 2026 after a five-day preliminary hearing. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges. His private lawyers later withdrew from the case, and a public defender took over his legal defense.Celeste's family has continued to ask for justice for the teenager. Now, ahead of her 16th birthday, they have made it clear that they support the strongest possible punishment if D4vd is found guilty.The case is still ongoing, and prosecutors have not yet decided whether they will ask for the death penalty. For now, D4vd remains charged with murder and has pleaded not guilty, while Celeste's family waits for the California justice system to decide what happens next.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Blackburn murder arrest after two people found dead at house
articles.summary: The bodies of a man and a woman have been discovered at a house in Blackburn and a man has been arrested.
articles.body:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder after two people were found dead in a house in Blackburn.

Lancashire Police said the bodies of a man and woman were found at the home in Hardman Street in the town at about 08:20 BST, and a man aged in his 40s had been arrested.

The man and woman, who have not been named, were both pronounced dead at the scene.

Police said they were unable to confirm the victims' age but local residents told the BBC they were elderly.

Police said a dedicated team of officers had been assigned to the case, and were carrying out CCTV, house-to-house and forensic inquires.

The crime scene would "remain in place over the coming days", the force said.

Officers have also appealed for anyone with any information to contact them.

A spokesman said: "Whilst this is a fast-moving investigation, we are at the early stages of establishing exactly what has occurred and why.

"Detectives are continuing to work to establish a motive.

"However, we don't believe there is a wider threat to the community.

"We will provide further updates when it is appropriate to do so."

Local councillor Terri Mahmood told the BBC: "The community is in shock.

"The family is deeply, deeply upset, it's shocking to them.

"We don't want to speculate, we just want the police to investigate."
